steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
A transformer’s core idea is to let every position in a sequence “attend” to every other position, learning which parts of the input matter most for each output token. Conceptually it works like this:

1. Input Embeddings + Positional Signals  
   • Words (or tokens) are mapped to continuous vectors.  
   • Fixed or learned positional encodings are added so the model knows the order.

2. Self-Attention  
   • For each token you compute three vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).  
   • You score every token’s Q against all tokens’ Ks (dot products), scale, and softmax to get attention weights.  
   • You weight and sum the Vs by those scores—this tells each token “what to look at” in the whole sequence.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Repeat the QKV + attention process in parallel “heads,” each learning different aspects.  
   • Concatenate and linearly project back to the model dimension.

4. Add & Norm  
   • You add the attention output to your original inputs (residual connection) and apply layer normalization.

5. Feed-Forward Network  
   • A small two-layer MLP (with activation) independently applied to each position.  
   • Again followed by residual add & layer norm.

6. Stacking Layers  
   • You stack many such blocks for deep compositionality.

7. Encoder vs. Decoder  
   • Encoders use full self-attention.  
   • Decoders mask future tokens in self-attention and also attend to the encoder’s outputs.

All training is end-to-end on large text corpora, using gradient descent to shape the attention patterns. The result: a highly parallelizable model that captures context across long spans.
